newsitem.title: USA: US foreign crudes muted, Algerian cargo distressed.
newsitem.headline: US foreign crudes muted, Algerian cargo distressed.

text.p: The U.S. foreign crude scene was muted on Tuesday except for a distressed Saharan Blend cargo whose fate was still up in the air, traders said.
Trading house Nova was still offering the cargo for early June arrival, although the exact dates were said to have shifted slightly to June 6-8 delivery from an original June 1-5 period.
The light sweet crude was unfamiliar to most U.S. refiners, who are mostly accustomed to running West African and North Sea sweet grades.
The price was fuzzy, although several traders pegged it around $1.25 a barrel under West Texas Intermediate/Cushing.
The foreign crude market was otherwise sleepy, with a narrow trasnatlantic arbitrage all but drying up offers for Brent.
The July spread between WTI and Brent was around $1.40 a barrel, down five to 10 cents from Monday.
Dated Brent, however, traded sharply weaker at July Brent minus 44 cents for a cargo loading June 10-12, down seven cents from a deal on Monday.
From West Africa, a U.S. equity producer was heard offering a VLCC of Qua Iboe arriving at the end of June, asking around 40 cents a barrel over dated Brent.
Plenty of West African barrels such as Qua Iboe, Forcados and Brass River were seen offered in July.
From the Mideast, Washington officially came out in support of a renewal of the Iraqi oil-for-food program for another six months, giving sour crudes a slightly bearish hue, traders said.
Venezuelan Mesa-30 was pegged around $3.00-3.50 under WTI for July loading, traders said.

From Colombia, a spokesperson for equity producer British Petroleum said Tuesday that Cusiana output will rise to between 250,000 and 300,000 barrels per day (bpd) within the next two months, from 185,000 bpd currently.

The announcement was in line with expectations that Cusiana loadings will increase in August from a current average of around seven cargoes. It was still unclear, however, how many extra loadings would come on the market.
The spokesperson also said, however, that guerrilla attacks had halted development work on Cupiagua, Cusiana's sister field in the foothills region.
Overall, U.S. refiners were still enjoying a wide selection of crude. "Take your pick, you can buy whatever you want to buy," a Gulf Coast buyer said.
Another was slightly more cautious. "It's a balanced to long market. Things are getting done, but it's taking longer to get done. It's well supplied."

One refiner also warned that margins were softening. "We had really good margins two or three months ago and they're still decent compared to what we've had, but I can see some problems down the road."
The May average for nationwide refining margins was around $4.00 compared to $4.67 in April, trade sources said.
